column3: It repeats the focus verse's paired denial: no faction can help, and the person cannot save himself.
It presents the earth swallowing evildoers as an unforeseen divine punishment, directly illuminating the focus event.
Divine guidance and help amid prophetic opposition only broadly contrasts with Qarun's failed protection.
Its catalogue explicitly includes people swallowed by the earth for their sins and denies divine injustice.
The immediate aftermath interprets Qarun's collapse as a correction to envy and self-secure wealth.
The question exposes a moment when a presumed network of mutual help can no longer act.
It directly denies any patrons besides Allah who could rescue those under judgment.
The promised empowerment of the oppressed begins the surah's reversal of Pharaoh's apparent security.
Remembering the final abode does not clarify the subsidence, failed aid, or house in the focus verse.
It joins inability to evade divine power with the absence of protectors besides Allah.
Unsupported worship leaves wrongdoers without a helper, clarifying the futility of alternative reliance.
Punishment penetrating through dwellings supplies a related image of judgment reaching a people's habitation.
It makes the apparently stable earth itself liable to swallow those who feel secure.
Pharaoh and his forces are seized and cast down, a nearby surah instance of arrogant power reversed.
Lot's request for help against corrupters does not add to the focus verse's collapse or failed rescue.
Those humiliated by Allah have no one able to restore their honor, paralleling irreversible abasement.
It explicitly sets earth-swallowing alongside other threats, showing creation can cease to be a refuge.
Divine aid through believers in battle concerns a different setting from Qarun's unrescued downfall.
The alleged partners possess neither ownership nor supporting power, framing why no outside aid avails.
Pharaoh's tyrannical elevation establishes the surah's broader pattern of power being overturned.
The promise that messengers are helped is an inverse and general case, not Qarun's failed aid.
It denies that wrongdoing can find a patron or helper apart from Allah.
It warns against leaning on wrongdoers and couples punishment with the loss of all other protectors and help.
Divine dominion over life and death grounds the denial of any other protector or helper.
The tactical rule about turning in battle does not clarify the focus verse's subsidence or failed rescue.
It gives the surah's explicit moral frame: the final abode is not for those seeking elevation or corruption.
The loss of a helper after divine rejection is related but too general to add much after earlier parallels.
A small group prevailing by Allah's permission contrasts with Qarun's useless faction without sharing the event.
The boast of a united, victorious group directly contrasts with the focus verse's impotent faction.
It states that no close patron can avail another and that no help will be given on the decisive day.
Mutual support among displaced believers is an instructive opposite but not a close parallel to the judgment scene.
Pharaoh's claim to divinity and construction for ascent intensify the nearby theme of arrogant self-elevation.
It locates victory in Allah rather than visible means, explaining the limits of Qarun's presumed supports.
Its opposed factions and divinely given aid show that group strength is not self-sufficient.
The nullification of deeds together with no helpers gives a general judgment counterpart.
The permanent abode of deniers is a distant dwelling-and-punishment parallel.
The challenge concerning a claimed exclusive final abode does not explain the focus verse.
It warns that divine seizure can occur amid ordinary movement and cannot be escaped.
It explicitly asks whether alleged gods can help their followers or save themselves, matching both failed routes in the focus.
Inheritance of lands, homes, and wealth supplies a useful contrast to the loss of Qarun's house and possessions.
Even an earth-full ransom of gold cannot avert punishment, sharply limiting wealth as a rescue resource.
It challenges the supposed army that could help apart from Allah, directly exposing false collective security.
Corruption followed by a bad final abode offers only a broad moral frame.
Punishment for violent rejection lacks a close connection to subsidence, dwelling, or failed aid.
The prohibition on expelling people from homes concerns communal conduct rather than the focus judgment.
The moon's darkening shares a lexical form but not the earth-subsidence event.
It denies any protector or intercessor besides Allah, a secondary parallel to unavailable rescue.
It traces promised support failing at every stage, exposing a collapsed alliance network.
Wrongfully expelling fellow people from homes is only indirectly related to the focus verse's house.
The battlefield command not to retreat does not add to the focus verse.
It combines inability to escape on earth with the absence of any other patron or helper.
The response of fearful hearts to revelation does not clarify the focus event.
The test of a claimed special alliance does not add to the subsidence or failed rescue.
It makes divine support, or its withdrawal, decisive and leaves no substitute helper afterward.
The parable and its reception do not bear on the focus verse's judgment scene.
Pharaoh and his forces are seized and thrown into the sea, a further reversal of collective power.
It denies escape in earth or heaven and denies any patron or helper besides Allah.
Steadfastness before an opposing group is a remote contrast to the faction that cannot help Qarun.
The human desire to continue in sin does not clarify the focus verse.
Wrongdoers having no helpers supplies a general but redundant judgment principle.
Pharaoh's arrogant self-exaltation with his troops forms a nearby contrast to the collapse of presumptive power.
The self-reproaching soul does not add to the focus verse.
Noah's question about protection from Allah is a limited responsibility parallel, not Qarun's collapse.
Mightier earlier peoples are seized for sins with no protection, directly challenging confidence in power.
Misguidance and the loss of helpers form only a general moral analogy.
Creation's purpose and the warning to deniers provide a broad judgment frame.
The promise of mighty divine help is an inverse, general counterpart to the focus verse.
After punishment they cannot rise or save themselves, closely paralleling the focus's denied self-rescue.
No person can answer for another, ransom is refused, and no help is given at judgment.
The distinction between righteous and corrupt is a general moral premise for judgment.
Divine aid to an outmatched group is an inverse example rather than a close counterpart.
The unjust are struck and left fallen in their dwellings, closely joining judgment and habitation.
Universal dominion is paired with the absence of any protector or helper besides Allah.
A decisive cry reduces wrongdoers to debris, supplying another image of overwhelming judgment.
The alleged gods can neither help their followers nor themselves, exactly distinguishing both failed rescue paths.
The denial of purposeless creation offers only a distant frame for punitive justice.
Believers' trial and anticipated divine aid concern a contrasting context.
Creation with a fixed term and warning gives a broad temporal frame but no close link.
It again denies substitution, ransom, and help at judgment, reinforcing personal non-transferability.
The compact denial of both power and helper closely matches the focus's failure of self and external rescue.
A prayer for steadfastness and victory in battle is an inverse and distant parallel.
It identifies false gods adopted in expectation of help, clarifying misplaced reliance before rescue fails.
It attributes victory to Allah's will, limiting any claim that support originates independently.
The proud are punished and find neither patron nor helper apart from Allah.
Allah as the best protector and helper is a general positive counterpart.
The critique of imagined partners is related but does not specifically address help or collapse.
It denies the efficacy of both personal schemes and outside help when judgment arrives.
The improper division of crops and livestock among partners does not add to the focus verse.
Allah's sufficient protection and help is a broad positive counterpart.
Divine ownership and severe punishment provide only a general setting.
The punishment of criminals and its stated outcome supplies another concrete judgment exemplar.
At final reckoning no helpers can interrupt the punishment or reverse their abandoned refuge.
The tempter admits that neither side can rescue the other, exposing mutual helplessness after judgment.
The command not to cry out because no help will come captures the finality of unavailable rescue.
Mutual counsel in patience and mercy does not clarify the focus verse.
Believers' reciprocal shelter and help form an opposite case, not Qarun's failed support.
It insists that those punished wronged themselves, clarifying the justice of irreversible judgment.
The closing prayer for aid is a general positive appeal rather than a parallel to the focus event.
The warning to enjoy their homes only briefly before an inescapable promise links dwelling to imminent punishment.
The deities adopted as intercessors disappear when needed and cannot provide the expected rescue.
It introduces Qarun's transgression and exceptional store of wealth, the immediate setting for his collapse.
It directly corrects the misuse of divinely given wealth by forbidding corruption and commanding beneficence.
Qarun's claim that his wealth came through his own knowledge exposes the self-attribution overturned in the focus verse.
His splendid public display and the crowd's envy make clear what his subsidence decisively reverses.
Those given knowledge answer the desire for Qarun's position with the superior and enduring divine reward.
It directly joins luxuriant living, destroyed towns, abandoned dwellings, and inheritance after their people vanish.
It qualifies such destruction by warning and injustice, framing the justice of the surrounding Qarun account.
The garden owner's fruits are destroyed, making his wealth useless just before the exact no-faction, no-self-rescue statement.
It warns that the earth may swallow people and that they will find no protector to answer for them.
It points to houses left empty because of wrongdoing, a direct habitation-and-judgment counterpart.
An earthquake seizes the wrongdoers and leaves them fallen in their homes, closely paralleling irreversible ruin at a dwelling.
An earthquake leaves the people of Thamud fallen in their homes, directly combining earth judgment and habitation.
An earthquake leaves Shuayb's people fallen in their homes, another direct dwelling-centered punishment account.
The cry seizes Thamud and leaves them fallen in their homes, reinforcing the same finality of judgment.
It states that what the people used to earn could not avail them, directly limiting accumulated wealth as protection.
Mightier generations are destroyed for sins and replaced, placing material endowment within a pattern of reversible power.
It recounts towns destroyed while their people were at rest, supplying a direct precedent for sudden communal ruin.
